overview: The Basques are a continuing people, not a kingdom that existed only from 500 to 600. This map’s outline spreads too far across northern Iberia to serve as a reliable linguistic or political border. The early medieval western Pyrenees were a region of movement, exchange and competing powers. Archaeology illuminates local communities, while their exact languages and identities cannot simply be read from their belongings.

periods.title: Early medieval communities
periods.summary: Cemeteries reveal connections across the Pyrenees during a period of changing regional identities.

periods.title: Basque enters print
periods.summary: Etxepare’s book gives a later regional voice a lasting place in print.

sections.title: Evidence close to the map’s century

items.text: A drought in 1987 exposed human remains and objects on the shore of the Ullibarri-Gamboa reservoir. The discovery led to excavation of Aldaieta’s sixth- and seventh-century cemetery. Lower water had briefly opened a window into a much older landscape.

At San Pelayo in Dulantzi, a sixth- or seventh-century burial preserved amber necklace beads. Their forms resemble those found at Aldaieta. Small personal ornaments help archaeologists compare communities across the region, even when the people themselves left no written biography.

Another San Pelayo burial retained metal fittings from a wooden bowl, alongside rounded pottery vessels. The bowl fittings resemble examples from cemeteries around the Rhine and Loire. Wood often disappears underground, while its metal parts keep a clue to the missing object’s shape.

sections.title: Food and farming in the wider medieval period

items.text: A study of fifth- to ninth-century rural communities found that the sampled Basque-region diets relied heavily on plants, including substantial amounts of millet. Researchers investigated chemical signals in bones. These reveal broad food patterns rather than the recipe for a particular family’s supper.

The same study found no simple rule that a grander burial meant a richer diet. Even people buried in silos or wells often ate the same broad kinds of food as other community members. A grave’s location and the meals of a lifetime tell different parts of a person’s story.

At Zornoztegi and Aistra, researchers tested 50 samples of charred seeds spanning the fourth to fourteenth centuries. Wheat and barley generally grew with low or moderate water availability and little evidence of manure. The burnt seeds preserve traces of farming decisions long after the fields have changed.

The seed study also suggests that farmers may have rotated crops with legumes to replenish soil. This remains an interpretation to test with more evidence. A field could need a change of crop, just as a household needed more than one kind of food.

Medieval Zornoztegi appears as a farming village without obvious differences between family groups, while Aistra has evidence of local elites and may have collected dues. Comparing their crops helps researchers ask who grew food, who received it and how much work households invested.

In 1545, Bernat Etxepare published the first printed Basque book in Bordeaux. Its fifteen poems include religious verse, love poetry and reflections on his imprisonment. The language comes from the Garazi area of Lower Navarre, giving a particular regional voice a place in print.

Writing sample: “Euskara, jalgi hadi mundura” means “Euskara, go forth into the world.” The Etxepare Institute prints this as its motto, echoing the poet’s invitation to his language. This attested modern spelling is used in the Institute’s publication; Etxepare’s sixteenth-century spellings differed.

Etxepare’s book used spellings such as “heuscara” for the language’s name and “beçala” for “like” or “similar to.” The sole known surviving copy is held in France’s national library. A whole literary milestone now depends on the survival of one small book.

For the later Basque whaling ship San Juan, historian Selma Huxley followed documentary clues in Spanish archives before underwater archaeologists found the wreck at Red Bay in 1978. Written records and surviving ship timbers could then be studied together, connecting names on paper with the craft of shipbuilding.

Basque cultural life continues through writers, filmmakers, musicians and language learning. The Etxepare Institute supports this work internationally. The map’s sixth-century endpoint is therefore a limit of this particular imported record, not the end of Basque people or their language.

ending.text: Basque communities and their language continue. Their histories passed through many political institutions and borders; the map’s 600 endpoint is not a collective conquest or extinction date.
